[判断类] The worker's §五.1-3 covers all three questions. My own checks add the following. Q1: ledger.md:52 already lists ~/.dsh/AGENTS.md. The audit only checks whether a file was recorded that day, not one row per edit, so it will not force a new row for every edit. The actual risk is the reverse. One row that mentions ~/.dsh/AGENTS.md covers every later change to it that day, so it becomes a pass-everything token. And if a session only touches the resident layer, the worker has to invent a 'delivery unit', which pads the sampling pool. Ledger bloat is not the main problem; the token pre-clearing changes is. Q2: the worker frames it as 'a suspect might be taken for a false positive'. The more dangerous order is the one actually used this round. The tokens were already in ledger line 52 from round 1, while those files were still out of scope, so the output is LEDGER_OK both before and after adding the roots. Without the erase probe, 'the root was never wired in' and 'it was already covered' would look exactly the same. The only other signal is the +2 in the [scan] count (28→30, which I confirmed against round 1's DELIVERY.md:58). So any future root addition should be required to show both the scan-count change and an erase probe. Q3: the benefit is that allowedModels changes now have to go through the ledger. The cost is not the stat call. It is the 111 KB file being hot-reloaded and frequently edited, which joins the pass-everything token problem from Q1. If later edits only touch other sections of the profile patch, the ledger's filename-level granularity cannot tell them apart. It becomes a burden when that file gets edited automatically by plugin installs or version bumps, which would cause bursts of suspects.

nonblocking.what: The C2 SHA256 only shows that the ledger after restoring matches the original. It cannot show that the probe round changed only the two tokens; there is no SHA or diff of the probe ledger itself. Next time, also record the probe ledger's SHA and the number of characters or lines that differ, so 'one variable only' is proven at both ends.

The conclusion from C7 Q2 should go into TRIGGER-POLICY.md §二 or LESSONS: 'when adding an external root, you must show both the change in the [scan] external count and an erase-token probe; LEDGER_OK alone does not prove the root is in effect.' Otherwise the next time a root is added, an existing token will hide whether it is actually covered.
